parts.problem_md:
Electromagnetic radiation is emitted from a radioactive source. The radiation has a frequency of 8.6 × 10<sup>20</sup> Hz.

Calculate the energy of an individual photon from this source.
parts.solution_md:
To find the photon energy:

List the known quantities:

- Frequency, *f*  = 8.6 × 10<sup>20</sup> Hz
- Planck constant, *h*  = 6.63 × 10<sup>−34</sup> J s (from the data page)

Recall the equation for photon energy, *E* :

- $E=hf$

Substitute the known quantities:

- $E = ( 6.63 \times 10^{- 34} ) \times ( 8.6 \times 10^{20} )$ **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
A heated filament and anode are placed in a vacuum, as shown in Fig 1.1. The anode has a gap through which electrons can pass.

![22-1-m-q3a-sq-cie-ial-physics](assets/001-22-1-m-q3a-sq-cie-ial-physics.png)

**Fig 1.1**

A potential difference of 15 V is applied across the filament and anode.

An electron is then emitted from the heated filament with a speed of 1.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>.

Calculate its initial kinetic energy in electronvolts.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the kinetic energy in eV:

List the known quantities:

- Electron mass, *m*<sub>*e*</sub>  = 9.11 × 10<sup>−31</sup> kg
- Speed of electron, *v*  = 1.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Elementary charge, *e*  = 1.60 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C

Calculate the kinetic energy, *E*<sub>*k*</sub> , in joules:

- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}m_{e}v^{2}$
- $E_{k} = 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 9.11 \times 10^{- 31} \times ( 1.5 \times 10^{6} )^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E_{k}=1.02\times10^{-18}J$

Convert this to eV:

- $1 \mathrm{J} = ( \frac{1}{1.60 \times 10^{- 19} } ) \text{eV}$
- $E_{k}=1.02\times10^{-18}J=\frac{1.02\times10^{-18}}{1.60\times10^{-19}}\mathrm{eV}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E_{k}=6.4\mathrm{eV}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *It can be easy to become confused when converting between eV and J. Just remember, you can only either divide or multiply by a factor of 1.60 × 10*<sup>*−19*</sup>*.*

> *Going from J to eV, your value should increase a lot (so divide by the very small number, 1.60 × 10*<sup>*−19*</sup>*).*

> *Going from eV to J, your value should decrease a lot (so multiply by the very small number, 1.60 × 10*<sup>*−19*</sup>*).*

- $W=qV$

  - where *q*  is the charge on the particle and *V*  is the potential across the uniform field
- $W=e\times15V=15\mathrm{eV}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the final kinetic energy, *E*<sub>*k,f *</sub> in eV:

- $E_{k,f}=E_{k,i}+W$
- $E_{k,f}=6.4+15=21.4\mathrm{eV}$ **[1 mark]**

Convert this energy to joules:

- $1\mathrm{eV}=1.60\times10^{-19}J$
- $E_{k , f} = 21.4 \text{eV} = 21.4 \times ( 1.60 \times 10^{- 19} ) \mathrm{J}$

parts.solution_md:

- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}m_{e}v^{2}$
- $v=\sqrt{\frac{2E_{k}}{m_{e}}}$

Substitute the known quantities:

- $v = \sqrt{ \frac{2 \times ( 3.4 \times 10^{- 18} )}{9.11 \times 10^{- 31} } }$ **[1 mark]**
- $v=2.73\times10^{6}ms^{-1}$

Calculate momentum, *p *:

- $p = m v = ( 9.11 \times 10^{- 31} ) \times ( 2.73 \times 10^{6} )$
- $p=2.49\times10^{-24}\mathrm{kg}ms^{-1}=2.5\times10^{-24}\mathrm{kg}ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
A laser sitting at rest on wheels that are free to move produces 5.00 × 10<sup>27</sup> photons. Each photon has a frequency 3.95 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz.

Calculate the magnitude of the momentum in producing these photons on the laser.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Number of photons, *n *= 5.00 × 10<sup>27</sup>
- Frequency of each photon, *f *= 3.95 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz
- Planck's constant, *h *= 6.63 × 10<sup>−34</sup> J s
- Speed of light in free-space, *c *= 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>

Obtain an equation in terms of the momentum of *n *photons:

- $p=n\frac{hf}{c}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities into the equation to calculate the momentum of *n *photons:

- $p = ( 5.00 \times 10^{27 ) \times \frac{( 6.63 \times 10^{-34} } ) \times ( 3.95 \times 10^{14} )}{( 3.00 \times 10^{8} )}$
- $p=4.365$ kg m s<sup>−1</sup>

**AND**

- This is equivalent to the backwards momentum of the laser; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> $p=\frac{hf}{c}$* is the equation for the momentum of **one** photon, multiply it by the number of photons to get the total momentum. Momentum is conserved, so the forward momentum of the photons is equal to the backwards momentum of the recoiling laser. This is a closed system, as the laser is free to move.*

parts.solution_md:

- $p=n\frac{hf}{c}$

- $k g m s^{- 1} = \frac{( k g m^{2} s^{- 2} ) s \times ( s^{- 1} )}{m s^{- 1} }$

$\mathrm{work}=\mathrm{force}\times\mathrm{distance}$

$\mathrm{force}=\mathrm{mass}\times\mathrm{acceleration}$

> *And use these to find the SI base units of force and energy.*

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Scientists are designing a prototype spaceship, with a mass of 4.9 × 10^6 kg. Once it has left the solar system, it will come to rest relative to Earth. It will then be accelerated by 4 very powerful lasers, which will be aimed at 4 large sails on the spaceship. Each laser emits photons with a wavelength of 2.50 × 10^−12 m.

Each laser emits 7.5 × 10<sup>25</sup> photons per second.

(i)

[1]

(ii)

All photons are absorbed by the sails. Calculate the force applied to the spaceship by all of the lasers.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
(i) To find the total momentum of radiation each second per laser:

List the known quantities:

- Number of photons per pulse = 7.5 × 10<sup>25</sup>
- Momentum of one photon, *p* = 2.65 × 10<sup>−22</sup> kg m s<sup>−1</sup>

- $p_{s e c} = ( 2.65 \times 10^{- 22} ) \times ( 7.5 \times 10^{25} )$

(ii) To find the force applied to the spaceship:

List the known quantities:

- Momentum of photons from one laser each second, *p*<sub>*sec*</sub>* * = 19 900 kg m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Number of lasers = 4

Recall the equation relating force, *F* , time, *t* , and change in momentum, Δ*p* :

- $F=\frac{Δp}{Δt}$

Determine the change in momentum of the photons:

- Each second, the photons from one laser change momentum from 19 900 kg m s<sup>−1</sup> to 0 kg m s<sup>−1</sup>

  - This is because they are absorbed by the sails on the spaceship

Determine total force per second:

- From one laser, $F=\frac{19900}{1.0}=19900N$ **[1 mark]**
- From four lasers, $F_{tot}=4\times19900=79600=80000N$ **[1 mark]**

As 19 900 kg m s*<sup>*−1*</sup>* of momentum is lost **every** **second** by the photons, the rate of change of momentum is simply 19 900 N. parts.solution_md:
To find speed after an hour:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of spaceship, *m*  = 4.9 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg
- Force applied by lasers, *F*<sub>*tot*</sub>  = 79 600 N

Use Newton's second law:

- $F_{tot}=ma$
- $a=\frac{79600}{4.9\times10^{6}}=1.62\times10^{-2}ms^{-2}$ **[1 mark]**

Recall and rearrange the equation for uniform acceleration:

- $v=u+at$
- $a=\frac{v-u}{t}$

  - where *v*  is final speed and *u*  is initial speed
- Initial speed is zero
- $v=at$

parts.problem_md:
A photon has an energy of 1.78 eV.

Convert this energy into joules.
parts.solution_md:
To convert the energy to joules:

List the known quantities:

- Photon energy = 1.78 eV

From the formulae page:

- Elementary charge, *e*  = 1.60 × 10<sup>−19 </sup>C

Convert the energy:

- 1 eV = 1.60 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J
- 1.78 eV = 1.78 × (1.60 × 10<sup>−19</sup>) J
- 1.78 eV = 2.848 × 10<sup>−19</sup> = 2.85 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A photon has an energy of 1.78 eV. Convert this energy into joules. 1 eV = 1.60 × 10^−19 J; 1.78 eV = 2.848 × 10^−19 = 2.85 × 10^−19 J

Calculate the wavelength of this photon.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate photon wavelength:

List the known quantities:

- Photon energy, *E*  = 2.848 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J (from (a))

From the formulae page:

- Speed of light, *c * = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Planck's constant, *h*  = 6.63 × 10<sup>−34</sup> J s

Recall the equation relating photon wavelength *λ* and energy:

- $E=\frac{hc}{λ}$

Rearrange for *λ*  and substitute the known quantities:

- $\\lambda = \frac{h c}{E} = \frac{( 6.63 \times 10^{- 34} ) \times ( 3.00 \times 10^{8 )}{2.848 \times 10^{-19} } }$ **[1 mark]**
- $λ=6.98\times10^{-7}m$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *If you're required to use an answer from a previous subpart, it's better to use the **unrounded** value to avoid rounding errors in your next answer to be on the safe side (although in this case, using 2.85 × 10*<sup>*–19*</sup>* will still give the same answer). *

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A photon has an energy of 1.78 eV.
1.78 eV = 2.848 × 10^−19 = 2.85 × 10^−19 J

3.80 × 10<sup>18</sup> of these photons are emitted from a laser every second.

Calculate the energy transferred by the laser every hour.
parts.solution_md:
To find the energy transferred every hour:

List the known quantities:

- Number of photons emitted per second, *N*  = 3.80 × 10<sup>18</sup>
- Photon energy, *E*  = 2.848 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J (from (a))

Calculate the energy transferred per second, *E*<sub>*sec*</sub>* *:

- $E_{s e c} = N \times E = ( 3.80 \times 10^{18 ) \times ( 2.848 \times 10^{-19} } )$
- $E_{sec}=1.08224J$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the energy transferred every hour, *E*<sub>*hour *</sub>:

- Find the number of seconds in an hour
- 1 hour = 60 × 60 = 3600 s
- $E_{hour}=3600\times1.08224=3896.064J=3900J$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A photon has an energy of 1.78 eV. Convert this energy into joules. 1.78 eV = 2.848 × 10^−19 = 2.85 × 10^−19 J

Calculate the total momentum of 5 of these photons.
parts.solution_md:
The find the total momentum of 5 photons:

List the known quantities:

- Energy of one photon, *E*  = 2.848 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J (from (a))
- Number of photons = 5

From the formulae page:

- Speed of light, *c*  = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>

Recall the equation for photon momentum:

- $p=\frac{E}{c}$

Calculate the momentum of 5 photons, *p*<sub>*tot *</sub>:

- $p_{tot}=5\times\frac{2.848\times10^{-19}}{3.00\times10^{8}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $p_{tot}=4.75\times10^{-27}\mathrm{kg}ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**
